trivia: I have a horseback contest in which riders struggle to seize a goat or calf carcass and carry it to a scoring area while rivals try to wrest it away.
I have a winter kite-fighting tradition in which flyers coat their strings with crushed glass to slice through an opponent's line; children then race to catch the falling kites.
I welcome the spring new year with Haft Mewa, a sweet compote of seven dried fruits and nuts soaked overnight and shared at the festive table.
I was home to a centuries-old Jewish community; by 2021, its last known resident had left after maintaining the capital's only functioning synagogue for years.
I have Pashtun communities whose customary code, Pashtunwali, places great emphasis on hospitality, providing refuge to those who seek it, and settling disputes through councils known as jirgas.
I have a communal circle dance called Attan, in which the drumbeat gradually quickens and the dancers' movements become faster and more synchronized.
I have an oral poetry tradition made of just two-line verses; many are composed by women and can carry sharp, defiant messages about love, war or separation.
I share the rubab, a plucked string instrument made from dried mulberry wood; UNESCO recognised its crafting and playing as shared heritage of four countries in 2024.
I celebrate the spring new year in Mazar-e-Sharif with a ceremony in which a great banner is raised at a shrine; nearby hills bloom with red tulips for the Festival of Red Flowers.
I was once home to a language whose scribes adapted the Greek alphabet to write an Iranian language, even adding a new letter for a sound Greek did not have.
I have supplied deep-blue lapis lazuli from the Sar-i-Sang mines since antiquity; by around 3500 BCE, this stone was already travelling as far as Mesopotamia.
I have a 75-kilometre railway link connecting Mazar-e-Sharif with the rail network across the border; it moved about four million tonnes of goods in its first year.
I have a 2.6-kilometre road tunnel through the Hindu Kush, opened in 1964; its route includes avalanche galleries and became a vital supply corridor during the Soviet war.
I have a vast copper deposit beneath a Buddhist archaeological complex containing monasteries, stupas and settlements dating back nearly two thousand years; mining plans have threatened the site.
I piloted a mobile-money system to pay police officers directly by phone; in one trial, officers discovered they were receiving roughly one-third more than before, once salary middlemen were cut out.
I became officially free and independent in both my internal and external affairs after a 1919 peace agreement with Britain included a letter acknowledging that status.
I saw carpet weavers begin incorporating tanks, helicopters and guns into designs that had traditionally featured geometric and floral patterns after the Soviet invasion of 1979.
I saw a British-Indian column leave Kabul in January 1842 with thousands of soldiers and camp followers; only one European, the doctor William Brydon, reached Jalalabad.
I had a 2,000-year-old treasure of gold jewellery and ornaments secretly hidden by museum workers in a bank vault during years of war; when the boxes were opened in 2004, the hoard was intact.

I witnessed a lightning assault in December 1979, when Soviet special forces stormed a presidential palace in Kabul, killed the country's leader and installed a replacement; the operation lasted about 43 minutes.
I am the setting of a bestselling novel in which Mariam and Laila, born a generation apart, form a bond while living through decades of upheaval in Kabul; the book is A Thousand Splendid Suns.

I had remote mountain communities whose pre-Islamic religion included wooden sacred figures and shrines; in 1895–96, an army campaign forcibly converted the region, and its old name was replaced with one meaning 'Land of Light'.
I have Band-e-Amir, a chain of six deep-blue lakes held apart by natural travertine dams that are slowly built by mineral-rich water; the lakes became the centre of my first national park.
I have a high-altitude lake at Dasht-e Nawar, about 3,200 metres above sea level, described as the world's highest breeding ground for greater flamingos.
I have Shiwa Lake, a landslide-dammed lake in the high Hindu Kush that was measured at about 14.5 square kilometres in a 2025 glacial-lake inventory, making it the largest mapped lake in that study.
I had 2,596 glacial lakes and ice-surface ponds mapped in my Hindu Kush in 2020; their number had risen by about 32 percent since 1990 as glaciers retreated and new lakes formed.

I am home to a critically endangered salamander found only in a handful of cold mountain-stream localities in the Hindu Kush; researchers revisited these streams in 2017–2021 after decades with little modern fieldwork.
I protect a high-altitude population of the world's largest wild sheep; a large male can carry curling horns nearly two metres from tip to tip, and its range here is concentrated in the Pamir.
I have eastern mountain forests where camera traps and DNA surveys found a common palm civet, extending the known western edge of this species' range.

I have a remote village in my eastern mountains where a small group of Pashayi boys have created their own fashion subculture: pakol caps decorated with butterflies, flowers and even incense, embroidered outfits, henna-painted nails and surma around their eyes.
I have Kyrgyz families living in my high Pamir where unmarried girls traditionally wear red veils; when they marry, they change to white.
I have Kyrgyz herders in my Pamir who move between spring, summer, autumn and winter camps several times a year, taking their yurts and herds with them.

I have high-mountain households for whom a yak supplies far more than milk and meat: its fibres become rugs and rope, its hide can line a yurt, and its dung is dried for winter cooking and heating fuel.
I have remote Wakhan villages where many traditional homes keep a mehmankhana—a room set aside for guests, where travellers may be welcomed by families they have never met.

I am home to the Hazara, whose population history is distinctive: genetic studies find an East–West Eurasian admixed profile, with close links to several Central and East Asian populations rather than a simple descent from one conqueror.

I have some Wakhi homes in my Wakhan region where Nowruz brings an unusual ceiling ritual: people use flour-tipped wooden sticks to draw designs overhead, leave them there for the year, and burn the sticks when the next new year arrives.
I have Kyrgyz herders in my Pamir who turn yak milk into qurut: small salted balls of dried sour curd that can be stored for the long winter without refrigeration.

I have traditional Wakhi homes in which thick mud-and-stone walls, low ceilings and very few openings help hold warmth through long winters, while a central skylight brings in daylight and lets cooking smoke escape.
I once had street photographers who used the kamra-e-faoree, a handmade wooden box that functioned as both camera and darkroom, producing a black-and-white portrait in just a few minutes.

I have a folk practice in which a family may take a newborn to a shrine and ask a mullah to write a tawiz: a tiny paper bearing Qur'anic verses, folded or sewn into a pouch and worn on the child's body to guard against illness, harm or the evil eye.

I have a 35-article morality law published by my de facto rulers in August 2024; it requires women to cover their bodies and faces in public, bars them from using public transport without a male guardian, and requires them to conceal their voices in public.

I have an educational circus movement that began in a Kabul orphanage in 2002; its children learned juggling, acrobatics and theatre, then took educational performances across the country, reaching 2.7 million people in 25 provinces during its first decade.
